item.title: Back to the Future, Sherrod Brown?
item.description: Where We’re Going, We Don’t Need Hard Hats.
item.dc:creator: Sean Trende
item.content:encoded:
Note: These writeups are long. Your e-mail server may clip them. Click through for the entire article!

Welcome to our second installment of Senate deep dives. This one is for paid subscribers only so if you liked my Kansas overview (which you only had to subscribe to read), consider sending a few bucks to the guy who programmed the computer to make all of these maps and charts! As I said, the plan is to expand this series to all 50 states for 2027 and 2028, with congressional and maybe even state house delegations put into the mix, so your subscription won’t be wasted.

Today, it’s Ohio. As we did with Kansas, we start by exploring the state’s political geography and history before getting into the specifics of this year’s election. Former Senator Sherrod Brown is trying to win again in a state that largely moved out from under him. Here’s why it’s doable, even if it is a tougher task than you might think at first blush.

State Overview

As with Kansas, to understand the state you first have to understand the underlying landscape. The following topographic map breaks down the basics of Ohio geography (if nothing else, these deep dives are forcing me to step up my R coding). The eastern half of the state is the rugged back side of the Appalachian Plateau. The Scioto River, running through present-day Columbus to Portsmouth, swelled deep and wide as the last glaciers melted, carving a broad valley that marks the plateau’s western edge. Driving east from Columbus along I-70, you can still see this: the hills rise remarkably quickly east of Pataskala, a sort of Colorado Front Range in miniature.

But this half isn’t uniform. Glaciers covered the northern third of this plateau in the last ice ages, while the southeastern portion was left untouched. That area is characterized by rough ridges and deep hollers, where the soil is thin and the slopes are steep. This left a landscape where farming was always difficult.

The Ohio Company’s Marietta purchase in its southern corner was settled by New Englanders; the rest filled in from Pennsylvania and the upland South. The Seven Ranges, which was the first area of Ohio surveyed, was settled by Scots-Irish Presbyterians from Pennsylvania, with some Quakers and Germans mixed in. The inhospitable terrain meant that the region sold coal, clay, oil, and iron instead of corn. When these industries declined, there was little to fall back on.

The northeastern quadrant, by contrast, is rolling and smooth. When the glaciers moved over this terrain they wore down the ridges and dumped them into the valleys, creating better farmland and a more hospitable landscape. Much of this area was bundled into the Western Reserve, an area set aside for Connecticut after it gave up its claims to the Northwest Territory; the state later sold it to investors who laid out towns and attracted settlers. At the far west of the reserve were the Firelands, set aside for those who lost their homes in Benedict Arnold’s and William Tryon’s Connecticut raids.

These Yankees laid out towns that resembled their New England homes, often centered on a green edged by white, steepled churches, tidy shops, and, in the county seats, grand old courthouses. These were small farm villages that later adopted fishing as an industry in the lakeside towns; Lake Erie is the shallowest and warmest of the Great Lakes and has the largest fish population. Politics here paralleled New England’s for a long time: Whig, then Republican, supportive of Oberlin-style abolitionism and hosting Underground Railroad stations (Sandusky was the embarkation point for Canada in Uncle Tom’s Cabin).

The west and southwest are the Till Plains, which is why Ohio is part of the Corn Belt. Here, the advancing glaciers moved freely over an ancient limestone seabed, depositing dozens of feet of clay, gravel, and rock. The hills you see on the map mark areas where the glaciers paused, dropping huge ridges of debris that roll across the countryside. The ground-up limestone brought fresh nutrients, and as generations of prairie grass and forests died, deep topsoil formed on top. The middle of the region, between the Scioto and the Little Miami rivers, was the Virginia Military District. A southern counterpart to the Western Reserve, it retained Democratic voting patterns along its southern edge into the early 20th century.

item.title: Why the Mary Peltola NYT Story Might Actually Matter
item.description: Being accused of trying to rig a system while running to unrig a system could be unhelpful.
item.dc:creator: Sean Trende
item.content:encoded:
Scandals in America are weird. Sometimes, candidates are sunk by the stupidest whiff of misbehavior. Sometimes, candidates survive accusations that surely should end a political career. I’ve always thought that whether a scandal stuck or not depended on the reason people hire you to do the job in the first place. Someone like Bill Clinton or Donald Trump weathered scandals in part because America has always loved a good rogue and in part because those candidates were nominated despite their personal failures. Say what you will about a Clinton or Trump voter, they probably weren’t supporting these candidates because of their moral virtues to begin with. Other candidates, however, get elected because they “aren’t politicians,” are outsiders, or will clean up Washington. For them, the standard is different.

Which brings us to Mary Peltola. The New York Times reports today that Mary Peltola’s campaign attempted to find and recruit a candidate named “Dan Sullivan” to appear on the ballot. This wasn’t accidental, as “Dan Sullivan” is the name of the state’s junior senator. It was always a bit harebrained, as Alaska uses ranked choice voting, where voters can rank all of the candidates by preference. If you are unsure which Sullivan to vote for, just rank them first and second (the “real” Dan Sullivan is also plainly marked as “incumbent” on the ballot).

Poll Vault is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

But not everyone really understands ranked choice voting. It’s a quirky, new system. There are always people who simply vote for one candidate and leave others unranked (so-called “ballot exhaustion”). Or there might be voters who want to punish “Other Dan Sullivan” by placing him below Peltola, but instead accidentally rank the Senator beneath her. These voters are likely few and far between, but in a close race, it could matter. In fact, that’s possibly at least part of how Peltola won in 2022. Some 11,290 ballots cast for Republican Nick Begich named no second choice and effectively disappeared when he was eliminated, more than twice the 5,240 votes Peltola won by.

In the world of campaign scandals, this is a relatively small infraction and something with precedent, as the Times story explains. This is something of the consensus in Election Twitter today: that in the greater scheme of things, this is no big deal.

In most cases I’d agree, but this one might be different. The problem gets back to the distinction I raised above. Something like this wouldn’t dent Bill Clinton or Donald Trump, who people knew were flawed.

Mary Peltola is different. First, she is running in a state with deep red DNA. The state has sent two Democrats to Washington since the 1970s, both under unusual circumstances (Peltola, the state’s member of Congress from 2022 to 2025, is one of those two). For a Democrat to win an election there requires pretty much everything to go right. She really didn’t need to be discussing this the weekend before the election.

Second, the cynical election analyst response—that this is just what politicians do—is probably correct. But that’s exactly the problem: Peltola’s campaign is centered on the idea that she isn’t just another politician. Anti-corruption, “Alaska first, party second,” and not being a career politician are central to her image. The headline on her homepage yells “To Hell with Politics…Put Alaska First.”

For a candidate who is running explicitly on a promise to “unrig the system” (in her X candidate bio) to get accused in the New York Times, with text messages to back it up, of literally trying to game Alaska’s unique RCV system after denying that charge repeatedly (and still denying it) really is a problem. To win as a Democrat in Alaska you almost have to be viewed as a quasi-independent non-politician. Peltola had been executing the type of campaign that builds that image flawlessly.

Now, that image is tarnished. In fact, the most damaging accusations might be the campaign’s apparent attitude toward Alaska’s voters. In texts obtained by the Times, one consultant watching a focus group wrote “Do we have a scheme for you,” while a pollster flagged a participant as the ideal mark for the ballot plan. It certainly doesn’t help that Senator Lisa Murkowski, the state’s maverick-y Republican who leverages the ranked choice system herself, absolutely blasted Peltola in a statement this afternoon, accusing her of a “pattern of lies and coverups.”

People wonder “who will really cast votes on something like this at this point?” My answer: the sliver of voters who are still trying to make up their minds. Voters who are either Republicans trying to decide between party loyalty and a reasonably popular former representative, voters who are non-ideological and who vote on things like candidate image, voters who really believed Peltola was different. Do I think it will matter a lot? No, not really. But this is a race that is close, with Peltola leading by around a point. Like many races this year, it could be decided by a razor-thin margin. She won by around 5,000 votes in 2022. Do I think this could sway 2,500 voters? Probably? In that circumstance, this is something that could really matter. One thing is for certain, the Sullivan ads are being cut as I write this, and this will be a large theme of his final push.

item.title: Please consider pre-ordering my book
item.description: (Sorry but my publisher says I have to do this a couple dozen times over the course of the next year)
item.dc:creator: Sean Trende
item.content:encoded:
I wrote a book. Please pre-order it.

I wrote one back in 2012 (The Lost Majority, which I have to say has held up pretty well) and swore I’d never do it again. Writing a book is an exhausting, wrenching experience, and when all is said and done, it isn’t clear that you make more than minimum wage.

But it turns out that I’m a masochist! I wrote another one, The Normalcy Paradox: Why Americans Crave Political Stability but Get Chaos, and it comes out in February. Apparently pre-orders are super important because they all count toward first-week sales. Enough of them can push you onto bestseller lists quickly.

Here are some links, followed by a description.

Amazon

Simon & Schuster

Bookshop

Barnes and Noble

Basic idea: For the past 25 years, our politics have become increasingly unhinged and destabilized, even though most Americans want boring politics where they can mind their own business and the government runs competently and quietly in the background. That disposition hasn’t gone anywhere. What has gone missing is the machinery that translated those impulses into stable government. The book traces how that happened, from Clinton through Trump’s second term. If you want a book that tells you why the other side is evil and entirely to blame, this might not be the book for you, but if you want a (hopefully) thoughtful, wide-ranging look across the politics of the past 25 years that explores changes in elections, society, and even philosophy, I think you’ll like this one.

If you’ve found this newsletter useful, the pre-order is the single most helpful thing you can do. Thank you.

item.title: What Might a Miss Look Like?
item.description: Toward a Hopefully More Nuanced Discussion of Poll Error
item.dc:creator: Sean Trende
item.content:encoded:
I’ve been noodling on writing about poll error for months as we planned and developed this Substack. Yesterday Nate Silver published a good piece in Silver Bulletin that moved this up in the production queue. (Silver’s thoughts echo points that he and I have both made previously.)

Here are the core observations: Poll errors are unpredictable and look like a random walk. Polls have sometimes underestimated Democrats in important races. Pollsters adapt and sometimes overcorrect (as they did in 2025). Any explanation for such anomalies is as likely to reflect the writer’s biases as it is to offer an actual explanation of what is happening.

Poll Vault is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

Indeed, while I can come up with stories about why polls this year might be underestimating Republicans on balance (see below), I can also come up with theories about why polls are now underestimating Democrats on balance. One obvious explanation is that pollsters are overly sensitive about misses in 2016, 2020, and 2024 and have overcorrected for them, effectively solving for Republican turnout problems in their polls that will still exist in the wild. Another is that pollsters are simply weighting 2024 turnout patterns too heavily.

You should read his article and mine because it explains the baseline and then helps me (hopefully) nudge the discussion toward what I think is a more nuanced view of poll error, while still avoiding the pitfall of “poll unskewing.” This is what I wanted the eventual “poll error piece” to focus on. It grows out of what I suspect Nate Silver is getting at in a cryptic footnote at the end of his latest piece when he writes, “I’d say I’m considerably more worried about errors in certain key states than about the overall national picture being wrong.” I think what he’s saying is that while overall poll errors are unpredictable, some states have more systemic biases. Put most simply, polls tend to understate Republicans in red states and Democrats in blue states.

To examine this thesis, I used a cool new tool we’ve recently developed. On RealClearPolling, you can click on the “RCP + AI” button to find instructions on how to create a connector to (for now) Anthropic’s Claude or ChatGPT. From there, you can use these tools to better explore the RCP database of averages and polling. I had Claude conduct a massive data pull: All the final RCP Averages for senatorial, gubernatorial, and presidential races as far back as we have them. I then compared them to the final race results to calculate the error.

But dig down a bit, and you see a different story. Even though the polls were pretty good on average in 2018 and 2022, they still contained meaningful misses. In 2018, for example, the polls underestimated Republican performances in Florida, Indiana, North Dakota, and Missouri, while underestimating Democrats in Arizona and Nevada. In other words, just because the polls are generally “okay” in a given year overall doesn’t mean that there won’t be individual errors that might be distributed in a way that alters the outcome.

Fine, but all that tells us is that errors are random within elections, which doesn’t advance the ball any if we’re trying to figure out what’s happening in 2026. You take the poll topline in all the races but acknowledge that, even if the polling is accurate overall, some races might be wrong and the errors cancel out to produce the “correct overall” verdict. So what?

Here’s where things get tricky. As it turns out, poll errors show some detectable patterns. Consider the following plot. This takes the RCP Average in every race and subtracts the actual result to give you the error. It then arranges the races from left to right, so that the most Democratic state is on the left.

This should be straightforward, but: There are a lot of large red bars on the left, and a lot of large blue bars on the right. It isn’t perfect, but it’s a pattern. The same pattern appears if we account for overall bias in a given year by subtracting the overall year-average error. It also survives if you break it out by individual election.

If we average races across years within states, we see a less-noisy version of this chart:

So again, this isn’t perfect, which is part of why my conclusion is not “feel free to unskew in the red/blue states!” Some of these states also have relatively few observations, although the finding holds if you narrow it to frequently polled states.

For the social scientists in my audience, here’s a chart for you. For the rest of you, feel free to skip (or wade in) as it is honestly more of the same, but with a bit of stats sprinkled on top. This superimposes a LOESS curve over the data and again suggests the relationship that should have been obvious from the prior charts. If we restrict ourselves to races between D+15 and R+15 to try to minimize the impact of outliers, the finding again survives (LOESS is sensitive to outlying observations at the extremes; it is one reason the curve bends upward on the left side).

What makes this finding comforting is that it makes some sense. It doesn’t even require actual poll error. If we assume that undecideds at the end of an election in a heavily Republican state are, in fact, heavily Republican (which seems reasonable), you expect them to break toward Republicans, and vice versa. In other words, you’d expect this pattern.

But we can also tell a reasonable story here that is consistent with some things we’ve seen this cycle. Let’s say that Republicans really are reluctant to talk to pollsters, either because of low levels of institutional trust or because of differential response/ “shy elephant” effects (not wanting to talk to pollsters when the environment is bad for your party). You would expect that effect to be maximized in heavily Republican states this year (where there are more Republicans), but to have relatively little effect in heavily Democratic states (where Republicans are rarer to begin with). You’d expect to see red states present as surprisingly competitive, while blue states look sort of “normal.” It’s a two-way street as well; Red California in 2010 and Red Washington in 2022 make more sense in light of this phenomenon.

Why does this matter? It matters because this year’s Senate races are being fought mostly on particularly red turf. Except for North Carolina, Michigan, and Maine (which, you’ll recall, is an outlier with respect to poll error), these are all pretty red states. To make this point a little crisper, I used our Claude tool to pull the RCP Averages for 10 states, selected completely at random: Maine, North Carolina, Texas, Ohio, Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, South Carolina, and Florida.

You might not be able to read the particulars well, which is fine with me—I don’t want you to build in a mental points cushion in each state. The pattern is pretty obvious, though. Note that in some races we did not run final RCP Averages. So, for example, there is no RCP Average for Iowa in 2024 or Kansas/Maine in 2020. Pollsters basically stopped polling South Carolina in 2020 in September, for some reason. Had there been averages, though, they would be consistent with these findings. In any event, poll errors in these states haven’t been confined to presidential years and have been fairly consistent. Notably, and contrary to popular discourse, Susan Collins’ overperformances can’t really be written off as “just about COVID in 2020.” She’s a serial overperformer. The following chart provides a more detailed breakdown of these races:

So what does the discerning observer do with all this? Here is where I think it gets tricky. This is a more nuanced argument about poll error, but I don’t think it’s fundamentally different. Situations change, and pollsters alter their tactics (every Maine pollster knows that Collins is a serial overperformer now, if they didn’t before), within states and in general. South Carolina consistently understated Democrats until it started understating Republicans. Alaska had some of the worst pro-Democratic poll errors in the nation before basically nailing 2014 (this is before ranked-choice voting added a new degree of difficulty).

Adding in a state-level “fudge factor” is a just-so story with fancier math. Or if you prefer, the road to “unskewed polls” is littered with credible storylines (I should add, “unskewed polls” is an old poll aggregation mistake; it is not a good thing!).

Instead, I think this should adjust your priors a bit about how you view the polls, not so much for your prediction, but for your uncertainty. In a swing state, the polls will probably be off, but it is harder to predict in which way. As a state gets redder and redder (or bluer and bluer), a “poll error” explanation becomes increasingly plausible for strange data. Put differently, as a state gets redder or bluer, it becomes increasingly less accurate to say “the miss is just as likely to be high as it is low.” I’ll spare you another chart, but this statement is eerily true for races in swing states (which produce an almost perfectly symmetrical distribution of errors), but the errors are skewed in more partisan states (note that this cancels out in the aggregate to “accurate polls”). So it shouldn’t affect your prediction, but it can affect your confidence in that prediction.

A stats professor once described statistical tools to one of my classes as akin to flying with instruments: You will almost always do better with them than without. At the same time, they have real limitations, and at some point, the best explanation increasingly becomes that something is going on in the data process that is mucking up your controls.

Regardless, if you want to know what keeps me awake at night this year, as someone who recently ran polls here (about which more in a later post) it was when Lakshya Jain at The Argument observed that the people not completing their surveys were different than those who completed them. Of course, pollsters can try to compensate for this (The Argument includes partial completions, but not everyone does), pollsters may overcompensate, and this might just as easily tell us something useful about who doesn’t vote as it does about people who don’t take polls. But there’s also only but so much you can weight your way around. That doesn’t mean that I add points to red state polls. It does means that I worry about them more.

item.title: Paid Subscriber Briefing Tomorrow: Levee Math
item.description: A live Zoom walk-through of the House map, the most important chart of the election, and some startling new polls
item.dc:creator: Sean Trende
item.content:encoded:
Yesterday, I posted the first part of my Level-Setting 2026 series, on the House. The short version: an eight-point Democratic popular-vote win would be historically excellent. But the 2026 map, with its valley of competitive seats and the redistricting “levees” on either side, may hold seat gains to something that looks underwhelming next to the topline.

Tomorrow afternoon I’m hosting a live Zoom briefing for paid subscribers to go through this in more detail.

What we’ll cover:

  • The history. How often do midterm waves actually flip seats deep in the other party’s territory? We’ll go through 1994, 2006, 2010, 2014 and 2018, and look at where each wave crested when normalized for partisan lean (PVI) and why the seats past that line are so hard to move.

  • What it means for 2026. Why the shape of this year’s map matters as much as the generic ballot, and what range of seat gains is realistic.

  • New data. We will have fresh polling in several 2026 House races that bears directly on whether the levees hold. We’ll go through it for the first time on the call.

Bring questions. We’ll leave time at the end for Q&A.

When: Wednesday, October 21st, at 2 PM ET
Where: Zoom, link below for paid subscribers

If you can’t make it live, I’ll be uploading a recording to Substack to send to paid subscribers afterward.

item.title: Level-Setting 2026. Part I: The House.
item.dc:creator: Sean Trende
item.content:encoded:
One thing I’ve noticed in early voting analysis (which you should avoid, but of course won’t) is that analysts often seem to see the data differently than I do. Someone will say, “This looks good for Democrats,” and I will think, “Uh, this isn’t what you’d expect to see if Democrats were gaining 40 House seats and eight Senate seats.” What’s more interesting is that I know many of these analysts and talk to them offline. When I do talk to them, it turns out that we usually agree, roughly, on where things stand. Our only disagreement is about what “good” for Democrats means.

It has dawned on me that, amid all the excitement over the 2026 election and the shape this wave might take, we’ve lost sight of what “good” means. That often happens in wave elections. In 2010, Gallup published generic-ballot results showing Republicans leading the popular vote by 15 points; polls showed a close Senate race in California; and a Democratic pollster had Senator Patty Murray trailing in Washington on the eve of the election. Democrats won both races, and Republicans won the popular vote by 6.6 points. Oddly, an election that produced the largest midterm gains for either party since 1938 felt like a slight disappointment for Republicans on election night.

Poll Vault is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

I want to correct that for 2026 and will do so in two steps. This is the first, and it focuses on the House. What I want to emphasize is this: If Democrats win by the margin the polls suggest, it would be one of the best election results in several decades for either party. Yet, because of the playing field, it could yield limited seat gains. To be clear, even low double-digit gains for Democrats on these maps would represent an outstanding election.

Let’s start with the following chart. This shows the national House popular vote margin in every election since 1992. I cut this off in 1992 because before that, Democrats had a massive edge in the South, where voters still supported conservative Southern Democrats in congressional elections. Believe it or not, 1994 was the first election where Republicans won the popular vote in the eleven states of the old Confederacy. It’s a subject for another piece, but the realignment of the South was a gradual process, not something that happened at once in 1964.

In any event, what you can see is that elections that we commonly refer to as wave elections—1994, 2006, 2008, 2010, 2014, and 2018—feature the winning party taking the popular vote by roughly six points or more. The current RCP Average has Democrats leading in the generic ballot (which approximates the popular vote) by 8.3 points. If this holds, it would be the third-largest popular vote victory for either party since 1992. A teeny poll error could make it the second-best result. That’s a good night by any measure.

You can also see, though, why I’m a bit skeptical of some of the more aggressive popular vote predictions. The 2008 election, which featured a Republican president with a job approval rating in the mid-20s, historic Democratic enthusiasm and turnout, a financial crisis, two wars going poorly, and, well, Barack Obama, resulted in a 10.6-point Democratic popular vote win. Donald Trump isn’t popular, but our job approval average has him at around 39 percent, roughly where George W. Bush was in the 2006 elections and almost fifteen points ahead of where Dubya was in 2008. The “right track/wrong track” spread is at -31.1. This is . . . not good, but it is a far cry from the -82 spread in 2008. I’m skeptical that this environment produces a worse result for Republicans than 2008, when the world seemed like it might really be ending.

But I should emphasize here that “skepticism” is not the same as “ruling out,” and I can tell stories (mostly related to coalitional shifts and turnout patterns) why this election might see a Democratic margin that exceeds 10.6 points. To be clear, this is more of a “gut-check,” useful for interpreting data that sometimes diverge, than firm analysis. Again, the idea is just to level-set. Regardless, even a nine-point win would be an historic night for Democrats, while an eleven-, twelve-, or thirteen-point win would be unprecedented in the modern era. If we end up at seven or eight points? It would still be a great Democratic night, even if it ends up feeling a bit disappointing.

This leads to the real focus of this article: What might we expect in terms of seats for an eight-point Democratic win? For this, I dug into the Cook Political Report (with Amy Walter) PVI archives to find the partisan lean of every congressional district before the midterm elections in 2010, 2014, 2018, and 2022. To simplify, PVI looks at how a president performed in a congressional district, relative to his national showing. The idea is that in a purely neutral year where the presidential popular vote is tied nationally, a D+5 district would be expected to give the Democrat 55% of the vote. I don’t go back farther than 2010 because I really do think something fundamental shifted in our politics that year, where we became more polarized and when Southern Democrats became a more-or-less extinct species (rather suddenly). This assumption might not hold, but even if it doesn’t, it doesn’t change the conclusion of this article much. Also note that Cook has changed his definition of “PVI” over time; these numbers are derived directly from his website archive but may look different in earlier-published sources. I use today’s definition only to compare apples to apples.

Let’s start with 2010. I’ll have four charts like this, so I will spend a little time up front explaining what they mean.

The 2010 election was very good for Republicans. They picked up 66 seats while losing three of their own (Delaware, which Rep. Mike Castle had vacated to run for Senate, and then two extremely blue seats in Louisiana and Hawaii that Republicans had picked up through accidents of history). This chart shows the location of every Democratic-held seat by PVI. If the Republicans flipped it, it is a red square. If Democrats held it, it is a blue circle.

As you can see, almost all Republican gains came in Republican-leaning districts that Democrats had been winning due to historical circumstances. Many of these districts were in the South, and others were districts Democrats had won in the successive wave elections of 2006 and 2008. Of Republicans’ 66 pickups, 53 came in districts at EVEN or redder. This led Nate Silver to label the election, memorably, an “aligning” election.

Beyond this, however, Republican gains were more measured. In the “purplish-blue” seats—those from D+1 to D+4—Republicans won 13 of 32 seats, about 40 percent. That’s important, and those seats were critical for giving John Boehner a working, meaningful majority in the House. Beyond that, though? The wave sputtered. Republicans didn’t flip a single seat at D+5 or bluer.

What about 2014? Republicans won their largest House majority since 1928 (while flipping the Senate). We see a similar trend here:

Republicans started with a “cleanup” effort, winning most of the remaining Republican-leaning seats held by Democrats. They pushed a little further into “blue” territory, winning seats at D+6 (NY-24) and D+7 (IL-10). Both were special cases, but regardless, the wave realistically washed up around D+2 or so; the real accomplishment was holding onto the gains of 2010. Democrats also flipped a pair of R+5 seats, although both reflected special circumstances (a badly flawed incumbent, great challenger, and Democratic DNA for FL-02; a swiftly tilting district for NE-02); they also picked up a D+6 seat that Republicans had won in 2012 due to a fluke in California’s “top-two” primary system.

The 2018 elections flip the script a bit, as this is the most recent Democratic wave. The lesson is roughly the same, however. Republicans did manage to flip a handful of heavily Republican districts. Democrats, however, cleaned up in the Democratic-leaning seats and performed spectacularly well in the purplish-red seats, winning 71 percent of them. Some of this is because many of these districts were trending Democratic faster than PVI could catch up, particularly in Southern suburbs around Atlanta and Dallas, but regardless, this was what the most recent great Democratic year looked like.

Note, however, that the wave once again peters out around R+5. Democrats won a handful of districts more Republican than this, but for the most part, the wins stopped abruptly at roughly the same place the 2010 and 2014 Republican waves had stopped.

For consistency’s sake, I include 2022, even though that wasn’t a wave election. This is complicated a bit by the fact that 2021 was a redistricting year, so it is hard to separate a “pickup” from “unfriendly redistricting,” particularly where new districts were created or old ones were eliminated through reapportionment. But the overall lesson is the same: The parties performed well in districts on their own turf, but failed to break through beyond the D+5/R+5 lines.

In other words, even in wave elections, it has been very difficult to push into the reddest or bluest territory. Of the dozens of seats that have changed hands in midterm elections, only a handful have been deeply red or blue. Now, this might be a coincidence, but there’s a certain logic to it. The basic idea is that as you press further and further into red or blue territory, you increasingly reach concentrations of demographics that are inelastic—that is, difficult to persuade. You reach blocs of core partisans much faster, which makes it exponentially harder to make further gains in these districts.

This brings us to what I think is the most important chart of the election. It shows the distribution of Republican-held seats heading into the 2026 elections.

Note that quite a few seats would theoretically be available to Republicans, but Republicans are unlikely to win most of them in this unfriendly environment. They could become a problem for Democrats in 2028 or 2030, but for now, Republican opportunities for wins are limited to a handful of re-redistricted seats.

But look at Democratic opportunities. They exist, but Republicans hold painfully few seats in the R+1 to R+5 range. Are there enough to flip the House? Absolutely, and I’ve long said Democrats more-or-less won the House on Election Night 2024, when Republicans won such a narrow House majority. Democrats have opportunities to make significant gains, but Republicans seem likely to win at least some of these purplish-blue seats.

There just aren’t enough seats to get to a 2010/2014/2018-type of result based on these seats. To put this in perspective, if Democrats win seats at each PVI level at the rate Republicans won Democratic seats in 2010, they would pick up about eight seats net. A rate similar to 2014 would yield four seats. A rate similar to 2018 would be much better, at 23 seats, but that’s still only about average for an out-party in a midterm election.

In other words, numbers that might look disappointing at face value could be the result of a spectacular overall result. A 2010-type election might produce only modest seat gains while still revealing a substantial preference for the Democratic Party at the polls. This is what I mean about the need to “level-set” our expectations in light of the House map.

I should emphasize that none of this is proof that Democrats won’t make serious inroads into these R+6 or better districts. There are clear opportunities to do so in some districts where Democrats have strong candidates and where demographic groups swinging heavily against Republicans are well represented (TX-15 is an example), while other polling data suggests these types of inroads might become a broader phenomenon. My point, again, is to level-set. Winning more than a few of these districts would be an extraordinary accomplishment. Coming up just short would be what you actually expect in a great Democratic year.

Note one other thing about the map, however. Both parties’ redistricting efforts hollowed out a “valley” in the most competitive range. Rather than spreading out their voters to maximize gains, both built substantial “levees” on either side of the valley to prevent substantial losses even in the face of a massive tsunami. But this strategy has limits. By piling up a mound of seats between R+6 and R+10, Republicans have created a map where, if the Democratic popular vote win grows large enough, Republicans could face a setback that takes years to dig out of (the same is true for Democrats in a substantial Republican wave). In other words, if the levee breaks, there’s no place for a lot of these Republicans to stay.

item.title: For the Love of God, Please Don’t Overinterpret Early Voting
item.description: Early returns are the “Elvis-in-a-potato-chip” of election analysis
item.dc:creator: Sean Trende
item.content:encoded:
Every two years, we reach September of the election year, and something terrible happens. Early voting begins. I don’t mean that early voting is terrible for voters or democracy or anything like that—I actually support early voting periods (of reasonable length). I mean that it is terrible for analysts.

It’s terrible for analysts because the data it produces is irresistible, addictive, and flawed. Why do analysts find it irresistible and addictive? Consider our plight. We spend years following every twist and turn as the election develops, while everyday citizens go about their lives. We can recite every candidate’s foibles as if they were a catechism, and we religiously await the dropping of the next poll, even as we understand the design limitations and inherent uncertainties that accompany modern polling. But once the early votes start to trickle in? We get something sorely lacking: actual election data.

Poll Vault is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

It is tempting to start drawing strong conclusions about the general election from these data. I am extremely tempted to do this. So, by October of the election year, I find myself writing some variant of this piece (for a decade now), urging you to please refrain from overinterpreting early voting (with one notable exception).

The reason for this is straightforward. Election results can be thought of as a sort of formula. You take a party’s share of the early vote and multiply it by the number of votes cast before Election Day, and then add the product of the party’s share of the Election Day vote and the number of votes cast on Election Day. This gives you the party’s overall vote total. So if you know these four quantities (number of early votes, number of Election Day votes, Party A’s share of early votes, Party A’s share of Election Day votes), you can figure out the election result.

Here’s the rub: Early voting gives us only one of those quantities, and only after early voting wraps up. All we really know is the number of early votes at a given point in time. Now we can use demographics and past precinct results to estimate the voting patterns of individuals who have returned ballots or who are identified as having voted early, but these are estimates. Worse, we know relatively little about the composition of the Election Day electorate.

This gets even more complicated because parties change strategies, and turnout patterns change. Early voting was a Republican-dominated affair in the 2000s, until Barack Obama’s campaign figured out it could use early voting to lock in voters, freeing up resources to target more difficult-to-reach voters on Election Day. This shift was compounded in Donald Trump’s first two campaigns when he (much to his advisors’ chagrin) urged his voters not to use early voting. In 2024, his campaign concluded that one of the party’s failures in 2022 was the lack of emphasis on early voting, and so the party changed its strategy. Early voting surged.

The upshot is that we lack a straightforward, stable baseline for cross-race comparisons. We see this in some online debates. You can compare early vote return rates to the rates at a similar point in 2022, but you’ll miss the shift in Republican strategy that occurred in 2024 (assuming that strategy carries over to this year). You can use 2024 as a baseline, but that requires comparing presidential years to midterm years, and 2024 could have been a one-off aberration in GOP voting patterns, with mean reversion this year.

On top of all of this, even if we somehow get the turnout rates right, we still don’t really know how these voters are going to vote. We can generate estimates based on poll data, demographics, and precinct characteristics, but we start piling inference upon inference to get our final estimate.

What you end up with is something of a Choose-Your-Own-Adventure approach to interpretation. I’ve written about this before, but humans are programmed to find patterns; it is one reason for our phenomenal success as a species. It’s how we figure things out. The problem is that we are all a bit overprogrammed to discover these patterns. It’s called “apophenia.” It’s why we find a man’s face on the moon or an image of Elvis in a potato chip or an image of Mary in our toast. In its more extreme forms, it is why we become conspiracy theorists, or why a gambler becomes convinced after sequential losses that she “is due.”

Multiple times, one group has looked at early-vote data and reached the opposite conclusion from another group. VoteHub has been tracking and modeling the early vote this cycle and finds electorates that have swung between two and five points from 2024, depending on the state. For example, they project that in Alaska the electorate will consist of people who voted for Donald Trump by 10.5 points. This compares to the 2024 result of Trump +13.1.

Of course, this is all contingent on modeling voting preference correctly, but my read would be that it is relatively good news for Alaska Sen. Dan Sullivan. I emphasize “relatively” – this isn’t good news for Republicans, and one theme I’ll return to in the following weeks is that our discussion about 2026 should really be confined to “degrees of badness” for the GOP. But given everything that is going on, running in an electorate that is a few ticks to the left of 2024 is something that most GOPers should welcome. Democratic nominee Mary Peltola probably can’t rely on Trump voters staying home to win; she’ll have to convince many Trump voters to send her to Washington for six years. Also, the fact that the swing in electoral composition is roughly the same in Georgia as it is in, say, Iowa and Nebraska seems to run counter to the theory that MAGA voters are disproportionately staying home and that red states are showing disproportionately large turnout changes. Whatever else can be said, at least so far, the same mix of 2024 voters is showing up in different states, without a disproportionate drop-off in red states.

Republican strategist John Couvillon (who has generally been bearish on GOP chances) has been tracking returns in states by party registration. I’ll start by noting that Couvillon is religious about warning against the dangers of reading too much into early voting data, but as of today, the votes are 50% Democratic and 29% Republican. That seems bad for Republicans! But at this point in 2022 the numbers were 51% Democratic, 30% Republican, and Republicans won the House that year. Suddenly, those numbers look less ominous.

You might take from this that I’m (relatively) bullish on Republican chances, but reread the earlier portions of this article. Of course I look at early vote data, and of course I form impressions, because it is tempting and addictive. But the point of this article is that I try not to put much weight on those impressions. It’s a siren’s song, and while I can’t reasonably fill my ears with beeswax, I can at least lash myself to a mast. Smart people I respect have looked at the same data this year and come to completely opposite conclusions about what they mean. I won’t rehash everything (you can read my earlier articles if you’re interested), but history is littered with the intellectual bones of analysts who have tried to forecast the general election based upon early vote returns. The Choose-Your-Own-Adventure nature of the enterprise is an invitation to find a pattern that may not exist, and worse, to force that pattern to conform to your prior view of the race (known as confirmation bias). Some people were correct on early vote analysis in 2022; they were notably less correct in 2024.

Even the more modest Couvillon data suffers from the “what is the proper baseline?” problem described above, and all of the modes of analysis suffer from the issue that we don’t know who is voting on Election Day. VoteHub avoids this somewhat by looking at voter propensity — how many previous elections the people who have voted so far have participated in — and drawing inferences from that. It’s probably worth its own article if I have time before the election; I’d call it better, but still not great. The bigger problem is that we don’t really know how these individual voters are casting ballots (what we call “persuasion”). If Democrats can win 15% of registered Republican voters in a state, a Republican-heavy electorate may be considerably less favorable to GOP candidates than the registration figures suggest. Mary Peltola convinced an awful lot of Trump voters to cast ballots for her in 2024 (while still losing). Maybe she can do it again. We don’t know, or at least we don’t know any more than we can surmise from good old-fashioned polling.

At the beginning, I promised to name one exception to my rule. That one exception is Jon Ralston in Nevada. The reason is simple and relates to the propensity approach I breezed past above: In Nevada, around 80% of votes are cast early. Nevada has registration by party, so by the end of the early voting period, we have a pretty good look at what the final electorate will look like overall, because Election Day voting is such a small portion of the total. We still don’t know how Independents will vote, or how much cross-party persuasion will occur. Another question is how large the Election Day vote will be. Ralston’s not perfect—he has missed on occasion, including at the presidential level in 2024—but his analysis was invaluable in predicting the state’s disastrous year for Democrats in 2014, as well as then-Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid’s seemingly improbable win in 2010.

So if you can’t help yourself, pay attention to Ralston’s Early Voting Blog. But unless you’re the Sage of the Strip (Silver State Seer? Sagebrush Soothsayer? I think I’ll let him pick), my advice is to relax and treat the analyses with a giant heap of salt. We’ll know the answer soon enough.

item.title: Welcome to The Poll Vault
item.description: Twenty days before a midterm is a ridiculous time to launch an elections newsletter. But I’m doing it anyway.
item.dc:creator: Sean Trende
item.content:encoded:
Here we are: 20 days away from the 2026 midterm elections. According to our RCP Average, Democrats lead Republicans by about eight points on the generic ballot. This is roughly the same as it has been for a month now. The president’s approval rating starts with a three (we can bicker about the next number, but does it matter at this point?), so it’s unsurprising that every model in America currently reads as some version of “Democrats will have a phenomenal cycle (unless [insert hedge here]).”

So it’s perfectly fair to ask why anyone would launch a newsletter about elections right now, when there is such little disagreement over the basic contours of the race. Even if you disagree, well, we’ll know in three weeks!

The answer is straightforward: At this point in the cycle, it’s easy for a reader to get trapped in a narrative, read polls less carefully than they should, and fail to stop and think about what the averages are telling her. The volume of polls coming in daily is about to go parabolic, making it harder for readers — many of whom are just starting to tune in — to separate the wheat from the chaff. Making matters worse, the participants in the broader polling conversation will probably split into three camps: the “model maximalists,” the “polls are gospel” dead-enders, and the “polls are rigged” dead-enders.

At RealClearPolitics, we’ve spent over a quarter century arguing against these views (in fairness, most modelers would separate themselves from their most literalist defenders), and I’ve been lucky to be part of that fight for most of that time. If you’re a reader who wants to know in the closing weeks (and hopefully beyond) what to make of conflicting signals, what the context for some of these races is, and why in God’s name Alaska has that screwball election system, then this is the place for you. We’ll talk a lot about things like poll methods, error margins, the historical context of races, the structure of elections, and the occasional thing that I just find interesting that doesn’t neatly fit into any bucket.

Who’s writing this

I’ve been the senior elections analyst at RealClearPolitics since 2010, which means I have now spent twice as long staring at crosstabs as I spent practicing law, and I practiced law for far too long. I teach political science at the Ohio State University most spring semesters (sorry, they take away my degree if I leave out the “the”) and I’m a Visiting Scholar at AEI—be sure to check out the Stubborn Things podcast I do with Jay Cost there. In 2021, I was one of the two special masters (people forget about poor Bernie Grofman, who wisely maintains zero social media presence) who drew Virginia’s congressional map. I wrote a book called The Lost Majority: Why the Future of Government Is Up for Grabs and Who Will Take It, and I have a new one, The Normalcy Paradox: Why Americans Crave Political Stability but Get Chaos, coming in February. More on that at a later date.

What to expect

Through Election Day: you’ll get at least two posts a week, and probably more. After that there will be a scramble of analysis for several weeks, and then we will probably settle into a weekly rhythm here. Eventually, redistricting fights, the 2028 primaries and general elections, and the occasional historical aside will provide plenty of writing fodder. Expect occasional detours into books, music, and whatever else catches my attention. I once spent more than three hours on a podcast discussing Van Halen’s complete discography, so you should have a reasonably clear idea of what you’re getting into here. In the end, I hope you’ll leave a post I’ve written with a better understanding of the election or argument in front of you, and with something useful to bring to your next cocktail party.

Some things to expect over the next couple of weeks, in no particular order:

  1. For the Love of God, Please Don’t Overinterpret Early Voting! I have written some version of this article almost every cycle for over a decade. It seems as though I will have to write it again.

  2. Eight Points of What? Why a D+8 generic ballot does not automatically translate to a gain of thirty to forty House seats (as it did in 2006 and 2018), and what that number might realistically look like.

  3. The Senate Contrapositive. Chris Cillizza and Chuck Todd had an interesting observation that I’d been noodling on for a while: If Democrats win the Kansas Senate seat, it probably means that we’re underestimating the wave. There’s a flip side to this that has received less attention.

  4. Ohio, From the Inside. I plan to do a series of in-depth analyses on key races, but since I live here, I can probably guarantee this article comes out before Election Day.

  5. What Might a Miss Look Like? Polls have erred in the same direction three presidential cycles running. What about this year?

  6. What Do Models Mean? We’ve all been living with predictive models since 2008, but what are they really telling us about elections? Where do they shed light on election outcomes, and when do they obscure them?

What I’m Asking For

You can subscribe for free, and a free subscription will get you a generous amount of content. But I do have to make a living, so some of what I write will be behind a paywall. If you find this work useful, I do hope you’ll consider a paid subscription. And if you know someone who constantly texts you while asking “is this poll for real?”, please send them this way (hopefully with a positive review).

Comments are open. Tell me where I’m wrong. It’s much easier to do here than on Twitter, since I won’t restrict you to 280 characters.

The vault is open.

— Sean

I’m also on X at @SeanTrende, where lately I post my Marginle score daily and fail to regret any of what I have to say, even when I’m getting dragged.
